distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of systemic sclerosis renal crisis.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: Diffuse cutaneous disease, sine scleroderma presentation, anti-RNA polymerase III, anti-topoisomerase I, glucocorticoid exposure, hypertensive and normotensive presentations, MAHA/TMA expression, and renal recovery context are represented as mechanisms, axes, treatment modifiers, risk factors, or case evidence; they are not extra disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Systemic sclerosis endothelial dysfunction, vasospasm, intimal proliferation, and vascular fibrosis create the substrate for renal crisis and other organ manifestations.
Renal arcuate and interlobular arterial intimal edema, proliferation, onion-skin narrowing, fibrinoid necrosis, and thrombosis reduce renal cortical perfusion.
Reduced renal perfusion stimulates renin release, angiotensin II vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and pressure amplification, even when absolute blood pressure is not frankly high.
Abrupt absolute hypertension or a major rise above a low baseline pressure causes renal, cardiac, retinal, pulmonary, and CNS target-organ stress.
Endothelial injury and arteriolar narrowing produce platelet-fibrin microthrombi, ischemic glomeruli, tubular injury, MAHA, and thrombocytopenia when hematologic expression is present.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: AKI, volume overload, and uremic toxicity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rapidly falling GFR produces rising creatinine and BUN, oliguria/anuria, electrolyte and acid-base derangement, uremia, pulmonary edema, and dialysis need.
Severe pressure and volume stress cause pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, myocardial strain, encephalopathy, seizure, PRES-like syndromes, and cardiac arrest risk.
Recent moderate-to-high dose systemic glucocorticoid exposure can increase SRC risk by worsening vascular, renal, and pressure instability in susceptible systemic sclerosis.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Systemic sclerosis vasculopathy is the permanent vascular substrate from which renal crisis emerges.
Recent systemic glucocorticoids can precipitate or amplify renal crisis in susceptible systemic sclerosis.
Narrowed renal arterioles create ischemia and stimulate renin-angiotensin activation.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Absolute hypertension may be absent when baseline blood pressure is low or cardiac output is impaired; a meaningful rise from baseline still carries diagnostic information.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Renin-angiotensin vasoconstriction and sodium retention drive accelerated pressure physiology.
Endothelial injury and arteriolar narrowing create the vascular TMA pattern of SRC.
Renal perfusion loss and vascular TMA rapidly reduce GFR.
Abrupt pressure stress causes pulmonary edema, cardiac strain, encephalopathy, seizure, and target-organ injury.
Volume overload, uremia, and acid-base disturbance amplify cardiopulmonary and CNS injury.
Prior or occult systemic sclerosis context is the disease substrate for SRC.
Skin thickening is common in systemic sclerosis but may be absent in sine scleroderma presentations.
Sclerodactyly supports systemic sclerosis context when present.
Raynaud phenomenon is a vascular systemic sclerosis clue but may be absent or unreported.
GI dysmotility and dysphagia are common systemic sclerosis organ-context clues.
Renal ischemia stimulates renin release.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Normotensive SRC can have only a modest absolute systolic pressure elevation.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: RAAS activation increases arterial pressure.

Dysphagia or esophageal dysmotility is a systemic sclerosis organ-context clue.
Anti-RNA polymerase III is an SRC-enriched systemic sclerosis autoantibody context; absence does not exclude SRC.
Anti-topoisomerase I/Scl-70 supports systemic sclerosis context and diffuse disease risk; absence does not exclude SRC.
Recent systemic glucocorticoid exposure, especially moderate-to-high dose, is a risk and treatment-context axis rather than a disease-name qualifier.
SRC often causes marked systolic hypertension but can be normotensive.
SRC often causes marked diastolic hypertension but can remain within or near ordinary ranges.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Very high systolic pressure directly raises target-organ injury hazard.
High diastolic pressure is part of accelerated hypertensive physiology.
Relative pressure rise can matter when absolute pressure remains below conventional severe thresholds.
Worsening renal failure raises dialysis need.
Preserved urine output lowers immediate dialysis need compared with oliguria or anuria.
LDH rise and platelet fall often move together through shared TMA activity, but neither is the primary cause of the other.
Schistocytes and low haptoglobin covary through MAHA.
Severe pressure injury can transition into PRES-like neurologic complications.
PRES-like injury can manifest as seizures.
Severe pulmonary edema and respiratory failure raise short-term mortality.
Irreversible dialysis-dependent renal failure worsens long-term survival.
Overly rapid pressure reduction can worsen renal perfusion and tubular injury.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hypotension, severe hyperkalemia, or intolerance can limit ACE inhibitor titration even though RAAS blockade targets the core mechanism.
A relative rise above baseline supports RAAS-driven physiology even in normotensive SRC.

side_effects.interpretation: ACE inhibition can increase potassium, especially in severe renal failure.
Over-titration or low-output physiology can produce hypotension.

treatments.context_specific_role: Targets the RAAS amplification mechanism and lowers pressure-mediated organ hazard while renal recovery remains possible.

side_effects.interpretation: Rapid or excessive pressure reduction can impair renal and CNS perfusion.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls acute pressure and target-organ stress in parallel with RAAS blockade.
Supports severe renal failure, hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia, or volume overload while the renal vascular process is treated.
Stabilizes pulmonary edema and respiratory failure while pressure and renal mechanisms are controlled.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reducing an active precipitating context is most relevant when recent glucocorticoid exposure is present.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes or reduces a recognized precipitating pressure on the renal crisis geometry.

treatments.context_specific_role: Can stabilize severe MAHA/TMA while diagnostic uncertainty is resolved; it should not replace RAAS-targeted SRC treatment.

risk_factors.factor: Early or rapidly progressive systemic sclerosis

early_rapid_or_diffuse_context.trajectory_modulation: Increases prior probability and speed of renal crisis expression.

limited_or_late_stable_context.trajectory_modulation: Does not exclude SRC, including sine scleroderma or atypical presentations.

positive.trajectory_modulation: Increases SRC susceptibility and supports systemic sclerosis context.

negative_or_unknown.trajectory_modulation: Negative testing does not exclude SRC.

positive.trajectory_modulation: Supports systemic sclerosis context and diffuse-disease risk.

moderate_to_high_dose_recent.trajectory_modulation: Can precipitate renal crisis and may worsen renal vascular injury.

risk_factors.factor: Low baseline blood pressure or normotensive presentation

low_baseline_or_normotensive_src.trajectory_modulation: Does not reduce SRC likelihood when creatinine rises rapidly and systemic sclerosis context exists; may increase delay and mortality risk.

risk_factors.factor: Baseline CKD, chronic hypertension, or low renal reserve

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises baseline creatinine and lowers reserve; ESKD hazard rises for the same vascular injury.
Can mask hypertension, worsen normotensive SRC prognosis, and amplify pulmonary edema and mortality.

delayed_or_inadequate.trajectory_modulation: Does not change disease prior but increases dialysis dependence and mortality hazards.

early_adequate.trajectory_modulation: Increases chance of blood pressure control and renal recovery.

supportive_care: Frequent blood pressure monitoring with attention to patient baseline pressure, not only absolute hypertensive thresholds
Daily creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, bicarbonate, urine output, urinalysis, hemoglobin, platelet count, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, and smear review during the acute phase
Assess systemic sclerosis context from history, exam, and serology without requiring skin disease when sine scleroderma is plausible
Use ADAMTS13, complement testing, renal biopsy, and autoimmune serology as structured diagnostic context; do not erase presentation evidence while waiting for them
Avoid or taper systemic glucocorticoids when clinically feasible, especially moderate-to-high doses in suspected or established SRC
Monitor for pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, myocardial strain, encephalopathy, seizures, and PRES-like complications in severe hypertension or renal failure
Renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia, oliguria/anuria, or pulmonary edema
Continue longitudinal nephrology and rheumatology follow-up for renal recovery, dialysis dependence, transplant timing, blood pressure control, and systemic sclerosis organ disease
